title: The Source Battlefield
subtitle: Where Scroll and Song Fought Over the Past
era: Memory and historiography of resistance, c. 1030-1600 CE
region: Ghazni, north India and Rajasthan's bardic archives
moral: Honoring the past begins by separating witness from legend.

sources.citation: al-Biruni, Kitab al-Hind, c. 1030 CE, trans. E.C. Sachau
sources.note: Ghaznavid-era outsider scholarship recording Indian learning with unusual rigor.

sources.citation: Prithviraj Raso, attributed to Chand Bardai; Hammira Mahakavya by Nayachandra Suri
sources.note: Later bardic/kavya memory traditions, valuable but not eyewitness chronicles.

sources.citation: Cynthia Talbot, The Last Hindu Emperor (2016); Peter Hardy, Historians of Medieval India (1960); Romila Thapar, Somanatha (2004)
sources.note: Modern historiography on source formation, bias and memory.

panels.shot: split-panel wide, left half a dim Ghazni study, right half a vibrant Rajput court

dialogue.text: Between al-Biruni’s quiet ink and Chand Bardai’s thunderous song, India’s wars lived on as a new battlefield: memory itself.

panels.shot: slow push-in on al-Biruni in three-quarter profile

dialogue.text: Around 1030 in Ghazni, while Mahmud’s campaigns were still remembered in dust and ash, al-Biruni bent over his Kitab al-Hind, determined to understand the land his patron had so often raided.
He wrote not of plunder, but of numbers and stars, of philosophies, rituals and languages, carefully weighing what he heard, warning his readers against exaggeration and careless hearsay.

panels.shot: medium shot of al-Biruni in discussion with an Indian scholar

dialogue.text: Drawing on Sanskrit texts and debates with Indian scholars, he explained concepts like zero, eclipses and karma, often praising what he found precise, yet noting where accounts conflicted or could not be tested.
Al-Biruni stood inside Mahmud’s world, yet his method was his own: to sift, compare and doubt, to separate what he had seen from what others merely asserted.

panels.shot: transition wide shot dissolving from al-Biruni’s codex to a Rajput court

dialogue.text: Centuries later, far to the south and west, another kind of history rose in Rajasthan’s courts, not on paper but in breath and drum: the bardic epics of kings and sieges.

panels.shot: low-angle medium on Chand Bardai performing

dialogue.speaker: al-Biruni & Chand Bardai
dialogue.text: “Hear now of Prithviraj, who faced the storm and did not blink!”

panels.shot: wide interior shot of the court audience

dialogue.text: Texts like the Prithviraj Raso wove Prithviraj’s battles, captures and escapes into long, ornate verse, binding court, clan and deity into a single tale of loss and defiance.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chand Bardai pausing mid-verse

dialogue.text: But the Raso as we have it grew over time; later poets added, reworked and expanded, making it a living monument to memory rather than a single eyewitness chronicle.

panels.shot: split close-up showing al-Biruni’s hand and a scribe’s hand

dialogue.text: One kind of text told readers when it relied on hearsay and where it differed from other reports; the other aimed to move hearts, amplifying speeches and duels that no one had recorded at the time.

panels.shot: medium shot of Nayachandra Suri at a later court

dialogue.text: By the fourteenth century, works like Nayachandra Suri’s Hammira Mahakavya recalled Chauhan rulers of Ranthambhor, blending record and kavya-poetry to lament defeats and praise steadfastness.

panels.shot: diagrammatic wide shot of a timeline in the background

dialogue.text: Modern historians note the gaps: al-Biruni wrote near his own time, while most bardic versions of Prithviraj and Hammira solidified centuries after the events they describe.

panels.shot: close-up of a modern historian’s hand holding both types of texts

dialogue.text: Using tools from Cynthia Talbot, Peter Hardy, Romila Thapar and others, they weigh these sources, asking: who wrote this, when, for whom, and with what hope in mind?

panels.shot: medium shot of al-Biruni and Chand Bardai rendered as translucent figures facing each other

dialogue.speaker: al-Biruni & Chand Bardai
dialogue.text: “Some truths are counted and tested; others are sung so they are never forgotten.”

panels.shot: wide shot of a battlefield dissolving into overlapping texts

dialogue.text: On the ground, defeats and resistances were brief and brutal; in the centuries after, they were retold, reshaped and sometimes magnified, turning short campaigns into long, shining sagas.

panels.shot: medium shot of a present-day reader in a library

dialogue.text: To honor those who resisted and those who endured, we stand where ink and song meet, testing legend against witness, and letting both tell us how people made sense of loss.

panels.shot: closing low-angle shot of shelves filled with Indian historical texts

dialogue.text: The past does not speak with one voice; it gives us careful observers and passionate poets, and asks us to listen closely enough to know which is which.
